subject: The Great Boston Fire of 1872
overview: Host Laura Duggan interviewed author Stephanie Schorow about her book on the Great Boston Fire of 1872. The discussion explored the fire's origins, the impact of a simultaneous horse flu pandemic on emergency response, and the legacy of Fire Chief John Damrell.

items.title: Guest Introduction
items.summary: Host Laura Duggan introduced author and journalist Stephanie Schorow to discuss her historical research and recent publications.

items.title: Origins and Spread of the Great Fire
items.summary: Schorow detailed the fire's start on November 9, 1872, in a Summer Street commercial building and its subsequent spread through the downtown retail district.

items.title: Impact of the Epizootic Pandemic
items.summary: The guest explained how a horse flu pandemic, or epizootic, incapacitated the city's fire horses, forcing firefighters to manually pull heavy steam engines to the scene.

items.title: Notable Historical Witnesses
items.summary: The discussion noted first-hand accounts of the fire provided by famous figures such as Louisa May Alcott, Alexander Graham Bell, and William Lloyd Garrison.

items.title: Leadership of Fire Chief John Damrell
items.summary: Schorow highlighted Chief Damrell's pre-fire warnings regarding poor water infrastructure and his later work establishing Boston's first building codes.

items.title: Preservation of Historical Landmarks
items.summary: The speakers recounted the saving of the Old South Meeting House and the post office, contrasting these successes with the destruction of the original Trinity Church.

items.title: Sylvester Baxter and Urban Planning
items.summary: Reporter Sylvester Baxter was recognized for his detailed fire coverage and his subsequent influence on the creation of the Middlesex Fells and regional green spaces.

items.title: Future Literary Projects
items.summary: Schorow shared details regarding her upcoming works, including an expanded history of the Cocoanut Grove fire and a novel set in the 1980s.
